opus-5.5.text:
Well, it changed it pretty dramatically, I'd say. So the backstory is that Kerenidis and Prakash had this quantum algorithm for recommendation systems, and it looked like one of the most promising candidates for an exponential quantum speedup on a practical machine learning problem. The input is a big matrix of users and their preferences for products, and you want to sample a good recommendation for a given user. Their algorithm ran in time polylogarithmic in the matrix dimensions, assuming the matrix is approximately low-rank and you have a certain data structure for preparing quantum states. And as far as anyone knew, the best classical algorithms needed time polynomial in the dimensions. So on paper, exponential separation.

I'd been writing about the "fine print" in quantum machine learning algorithms for a while: the input loading problem, the output readout problem, the condition number dependence, and so on. One question I kept raising was whether, once you grant the quantum algorithm all the assumptions it needs, including that fancy data structure, a classical algorithm with comparable access might do just as well. That's not a fair comparison otherwise.

So Ewin was an undergraduate at UT Austin, I think eighteen at the time, and I gave her this as a senior thesis project. Frankly I expected her to prove a classical lower bound, that no classical algorithm with that kind of sampling access could match the quantum one. That would have made the speedup more solid. Instead, after working on it for a while, she came back and said she thought there was a fast classical algorithm. Eventually she found one, a "dequantization," running in time polylogarithmic in the dimensions, just like the quantum algorithm. The key insight was that the data structure the quantum algorithm assumed also lets a classical algorithm do length-squared sampling of rows and entries, and with that, plus ideas from randomized linear algebra going back to Frieze, Kannan, and Vempala, you can do the low-rank approximation and sampling classically.

So the exponential speedup just evaporated. The classical algorithm had worse polynomial dependence on the rank, the error, and the condition number, so there's maybe a polynomial gap left, but not the exponential separation that was the whole selling point.

And it didn't stop there. She and others extended the technique to dequantize a whole family of quantum machine learning algorithms based on low-rank assumptions: principal component analysis, supervised clustering, certain low-rank linear system solvers. So the lesson I took was that whenever someone claims an exponential quantum speedup for a machine learning task, you have to ask whether the speedup actually comes from quantum mechanics, or from the strong input assumptions. Often it's the latter. It made me a lot more skeptical of that whole genre of claims, while also showing how valuable it is to seriously try to find classical algorithms, rather than just assuming they don't exist.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it changed it completely, and I'd say in the most satisfying way possible for a theorist, even if it was a little humbling for the field.

So the background: in 2016, Kerenidis and Prakash had this quantum algorithm for recommendation systems, the Netflix-style problem where you have a huge matrix of users and products, you assume it's approximately low rank, and you want to sample a product a given user would probably like. Their algorithm ran in time polylogarithmic in the dimensions of the matrix, whereas the best classical algorithms everybody knew took time polynomial in the dimensions. And crucially, this looked like one of the few candidates for an exponential quantum speedup on a practical machine learning task. Not factoring, not quantum simulation, but something a company might actually want to do. Many of us pointed to it as maybe the best example we had in quantum machine learning.

Now, I did have a nagging suspicion. The Kerenidis-Prakash algorithm assumes the data is loaded into a particular data structure, essentially a binary tree of squared norms, that lets you prepare quantum states corresponding to rows of the matrix in polylog time. That's what Ewin and I later called the "state preparation assumption," and I had this worry that the assumption was so strong that it might be giving a classical algorithm the same kind of superpower, if you looked at it the right way. So I gave this to Ewin, who was an undergraduate at UT Austin at the time, as a senior thesis project. The original plan was actually for her to prove the speedup was real, to show some hardness result. She spent a while trying and kept failing, and eventually she came back and said, I think the reason I can't prove this is hard is that it isn't.

What she showed is that if you give a classical algorithm the ability to sample from the rows of the matrix with probability proportional to their squared norms, which is exactly what that data structure lets you do, then you can do essentially what the quantum algorithm does, with only a polynomial, not exponential, slowdown. It builds on older work by Frieze, Kannan, and Vempala on sampling-based low-rank approximation, but she had to get around some real obstacles, and the result was a classical algorithm with runtime polylogarithmic in the dimensions. So the exponential speedup evaporated.

I'll say I was skeptical for a few days when she first told me. We had the result checked by Kerenidis and Prakash themselves, and they were extremely gracious about it. And it's worth being careful: the quantum algorithm still has a polynomial advantage over Ewin's algorithm in terms of the rank and the error parameters. It's just that the headline claim, the exponential one, is gone.

The bigger effect, honestly, is on how I think about the whole area. This led to what people now call "dequantization," and Ewin and others went on to dequantize a bunch of other quantum machine learning algorithms, principal component analysis, supervised clustering, some low-rank linear systems stuff. The lesson I took is that whenever a quantum algorithm assumes a fancy way of getting classical data into quantum states, you have to ask what a classical algorithm could do with equally fancy access to the data. If you don't ask that question, you're not comparing apples to apples. It's made me a lot more cautious about exponential speedup claims in QML, and it's a wonderful example of why you want undergrads around who don't yet know what they're supposed to be unable to do.

astra-6.text:
It made me much more skeptical of that particular proposed speedup. The quantum recommendation algorithm had looked like a promising example of an exponential advantage for a practical machine-learning problem. I suggested that Ewin investigate whether a classical algorithm could do something comparable, and she found one.

The crucial issue was access to the data. The quantum algorithm assumed that you could efficiently prepare quantum states encoding the input. If you give a classical algorithm a corresponding ability to sample from that input, Ewin showed that it could also solve the recommendation problem in time polylogarithmic in the dimensions, under the relevant assumptions. That removed the claimed exponential separation, although it didn’t mean the classical algorithm was necessarily practical or that every possible quantum advantage disappeared.

For me, the lesson was that you have to scrutinize the input assumptions as carefully as the quantum algorithm itself. If you assume a powerful mechanism for loading your data, you should ask what that same mechanism lets a classical algorithm do. Ewin’s work showed just how much could be hiding there.

sol-6.1.text:
It made me much more skeptical that recommendation systems would provide an exponential quantum speedup. The quantum algorithm had looked very promising, but it assumed that you could access the input data in a particular, very powerful way. Ewin showed that if you give a classical algorithm analogous sampling access, then it can also solve the problem efficiently, under comparable assumptions.

The wonderful irony is that I had suggested this problem to Ewin expecting that proving a classical limitation might be a good project. Ewin went in the opposite direction and found the classical algorithm. That changed the question from “Is there an exponential quantum advantage here?” to “What advantage remains once we account fairly for data access?” It didn’t rule out every quantum advantage, but it removed the basis for that particular exponential separation.
